opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really meaningful distinction, and honestly one that I'm encouraged to see. What we've heard from a lot of artists we work with is that there's been this growing pushback from the buyer side. Some publishers, game studios, and individual commissioners are explicitly saying, "We want human-made work, and we want assurances that it's human-made." Part of that is about quality and intentionality. When you commission a human artist, you're getting someone who understands your story, who makes deliberate choices, who can iterate with you in a way that's grounded in actual creative judgment. That's very different from sampling outputs from a model until something looks close enough.

But there's also an ethical dimension that I think buyers are increasingly aware of. Many of these generative models were trained on artists' work without consent, without compensation, without credit. So if you're a publisher and you put an AI-generated cover on a book, there's a real chance that image is built on top of the very artists whose livelihoods are being undercut. Readers and fans notice that, and there's been real backlash in cases where companies got caught using AI art without disclosure.

The tricky part is enforcement. It's getting harder to tell, just by looking, whether something was generated or made by hand, and some people pass off AI output as their own work. So you see buyers asking for process files, sketches, layered files, time-lapse recordings, things that show the work was actually done. That puts an extra burden on human artists, which isn't entirely fair, but it reflects how much the landscape has shifted.

From my perspective, this distinction matters because it's part of how the market signals what it values. If human creativity is going to stay economically viable, buyers choosing human work and being willing to pay for it is one of the most important forces we have, alongside technical protections and, hopefully, better regulation down the road.

r001.rationale: The response says buyers want human-made work and assurances, but does not clearly state that publishers exclude artists from those commissions because of AI use.

r002.rationale: It mentions people passing off AI output as their own and backlash over undisclosed use, but does not characterize selling AI-generated work under a human-made promise as defrauding buyers.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think what's interesting is that this is a market signal we didn't necessarily anticipate when we started working on Glaze. When we first talked to artists, the fear was pretty existential: generative models would flood the market with cheap imitations, nobody would be able to tell the difference, and commissions would just dry up. And some of that has happened, especially at the low end, the stock-image type work.

But what we've seen alongside it is that a lot of publishers, game studios, and individual buyers have started to explicitly distinguish between the two. Some of it is about quality and consistency, because a human artist can take direction, iterate, keep a character on-model across fifty pages, and a model still struggles with that. Some of it is legal risk, because nobody wants to find out later that the cover art they shipped is a near-copy of someone's portfolio. And honestly, a lot of it is reputational. Fans notice. Readers notice. There have been real backlashes when a publisher got caught using AI art and tried to pass it off, and that changed the calculus for others.

So the distinction buyers are drawing is partly about the work itself and partly about provenance. "Human-made" is turning into a label that carries value, a bit like "handmade" or "organic" did in other markets. I have mixed feelings about that, to be honest. On one hand it's great, it means human artists have a differentiated product and a reason people will pay for it. On the other hand, a label only works if it's trustworthy, and right now there's no reliable way to verify it. Detection tools are unreliable, and people will absolutely lie about it.

That's actually one reason we think protection matters so much. If an artist's style can be cloned in an afternoon, then "commission a human" versus "generate in their style" becomes a very thin line, and the label erodes. If the style is harder to extract, that distinction has teeth. So I see the market distinction and the technical protection as complementary. The market is saying human work is worth more. Our job on the technical side is to make sure that claim can keep meaning something.

r001.rationale: The response says publishers and buyers distinguish AI art from human work, but it does not state that publishers exclude artists who use AI from commissions intended to be human-created.

r002.rationale: The response mentions reputational backlash when a publisher used AI art and tried to pass it off, but it does not characterize this as defrauding commission buyers.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re buying different things. If you’re a publisher looking for an illustration to fill a space, you may care primarily about whether the image meets your needs and what it costs. That creates very real pressure on artists whose livelihoods depend on those commissions.

But when someone commissions a particular artist, the relationship can be part of the value. They care about that person’s perspective, the choices they make, and the conversation that shapes the work. A visually similar image doesn’t necessarily fulfill that same desire.

The concern is that recognizing that distinction doesn’t protect artists economically. You can value human creativity in principle and still move your illustration budget to generated images. So I’d look less at whether buyers say these are different categories and more at what they actually pay artists to do.

r001.rationale: The response says publishers may shift illustration budgets to generated images, but does not say they exclude artists from commissions intended to be human-created or that this practice is increasing.

r002.rationale: The response discusses differences in value and economic pressure, but does not characterize selling AI-generated art as human-created as defrauding buyers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re buying two very different things. If you’re a publisher and you need an illustration to fill a space, you may care primarily about how it looks and what it costs. AI-generated imagery can be attractive in that context. But when someone commissions an artist, often they’re interested in that particular person—their perspective, their experience, and the conversation that goes into creating the piece.

So I don’t think the distinction is simply, can you tell which image was generated by a machine? Two images might look very similar and still have very different value to the buyer because of how they were made and who made them. The concern is that the people making purchasing decisions won’t always value that distinction, especially when there’s pressure to cut costs.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts what publishers and commission buyers value, but does not say publishers exclude artists from commissions intended to be human-created.

r002.rationale: The response says how an image was made affects its value, but does not characterize selling AI-generated art as human-created as fraud or deception.
